title: How to Increase Dwell Time in Retail Stores | Entuned
meta_description: Five levers that move retail dwell time. Why operators undershoot the easiest one. A two-week test you can run on your own floor against your POS data.

faq.q: What is a good dwell time for a retail store?
faq.a: Dwell time benchmarks are category-specific. Fast-fashion sees 4 to 8 minutes per visit. Specialty apparel and home goods commonly run 12 to 25. Furniture and mattress stores trend 30 to 60 plus. The relevant question is not what is good in absolute terms but whether your dwell is moving over time and whether the customers who stay longer are spending more. Both are knowable from your existing POS and door-counter data.

faq.q: What actually increases dwell time in a retail store?
faq.a: Five levers, in roughly the order operators undershoot them. Layout and pathing that gives customers a reason to walk further into the floor. Visual merchandising at eye level that breaks the scan-and-leave reflex. Staff engagement timing that interrupts indecision before customers retreat. The audio environment, especially tempo and familiarity, which is the cheapest and most-ignored of the five. And finally, friction reduction at fitting rooms, checkout, and decision points.

faq.q: Does music actually affect dwell time?
faq.a: Yes, and the effect is well-documented. Milliman 1982 found slow tempo increased grocery shopper dwell. Yalch and Spangenberg 2000 found unfamiliar music made shoppers stay longer than familiar music. The mechanism is partly attentional — music customers do not recognize creates fewer time markers, so the internal clock runs slower. The effect is per-customer, which means it shows up in one store the same way it shows up in 50.

faq.q: How can I measure dwell time without expensive sensors?
faq.a: Three options, in order of cost. A door counter plus your POS lets you compute average visit duration as foot traffic divided by transactions, then refined by daypart. A security camera review of two hours on a Saturday afternoon gives you a directional sample for the cost of one staff hour. A simple stopwatch sample of 20 customers gives you a baseline you can compare against later. None requires a six-figure analytics deployment.

faq.q: What is the cheapest test I can run this month?
faq.a: Two weeks. Pick a baseline week with normal weather, traffic, and staffing. Pull your conversion rate and average basket. Change one variable for the next week — the music is the easiest one to change, since it has no operational lift. Pull the same numbers.
